title: Show HN: Toggles, a game based on analyzing data
text:
Hey, I'm Matt. This is a free game I built in the spirit of the old internet. Just built for fun and no other reason. I built a version 2-3 years ago by hand. This time I built it assisted by Claude Code.

Every day you set a toggle. On/off, dials, etc. Every single one of them follows some piece of public data.

The board locks at 23:00 UTC and is scored. You then find out what was right or wrong. On some toggles there's also an indicator if you are hot or cold. The goal is to get them all right :).

Hints are given along at checkpoints along the way.

I have an open beta beginning November 30th. Would love to get feedback on the concept, what works, what doesn't, etc so that season 1 goes off without too many hitches.

text:

Without the speed issue, Carbon would be a top model already. It's top on our battle system built on opencode, if you exclude early votes: https://agentduel.com/leaderboard?excludeEarlyVotes=true, though to be fair, small sample size so far.

title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
text:
Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses.

The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right.

The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome.

kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

title: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models
author: vighneshiyer

title: Re: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models...
text:
It will be interesting to see if AI really starts innovating in circuit design or just continues doing the wrong things faster. But I'd bet that it will soon run circles around the status quo, and rightly so.

We're way out on the long tail of a dead-end approach to computation that started in the late 1990s with GPUs when we chose to optimize SIMD at the expense of general-purpose computing. On top of that, Moore's Law ended in roughly 2007 with the arrival of smartphones, when the industry chose cost and power minimization over compute maximization via a multicore approach.

Now only servers have access to highly multicore chips like AMD EPYC, at 10-100 times the cost and with poorer performance than if they maximized local/shared memories with content-addressable caching. Apple's M line of processors is ok, but its specialized cores just stand in the way of the higher abstractions available with symmetric multiprocessing, upon which specialized algorithms can be built. We're still missing the multicore foundation.

I used Synopsys and Cadence back in college in the late 1990s to automatically place and route circuits from diagrams in SPICE (I think, my memory is foggy) and they already performed 80% as well as humans. I don't remember if that was for chip area, speed or power. But the big players were obviously using tools at least as capable as whatever we were trained on.

Then in the 2000s I had hoped to do what OpenAI is doing and simulate small/open CPU designs on FPGAs. But the economics just weren't there. Even though some people like me (the poors) knew just exactly what could work, there was a tech winter between roughly the Dot Bomb around 2000 to the start of the Mobile Bubble in the early 2010s. So we didn't have a way to communicate what was possible to the people with capital, without having to network to get through the gatekeeping. Which may be fun for enthusiasts, but it's anathema to hackers wanting to get real work done.

I'd nearly given up all hope of progress until last year when AI went mainstream. Now I see 3 steps to the epiphany:

[x] Time

[ ] Money

[ ] Resources

AI solves the time component, since specs (ideas) are orders of magnitude easier to create than implementations.

But money and resources may not be available for quite some time. It's looking like the music may stop for AI funding next year, now that the election is over and the writing's on the wall as far as doing things without consent goes. Regulation is coming, and with it perhaps the last AI winter, although admittedly I'm probably exaggerating.

So as usual, we may have to pull ourselves up by our bootstraps and skip the money step to provide resources directly to ourselves and the rest of humanity. There's so much capital now that all it can do is inflate Wall Street. There's little to no carryover onto Main Street. So in a very real way, it's easier now to make money by borrowing and investing than going to a job. That's a dangerous situation for any country, as it slips into being a giant casino of haves and have-nots. We'll let the farms go under before raising taxes.

The interesting thing is that without my involvement, the universe went ahead and made AI without me, which is ..surprising. But automating problem solving was perhaps the hardest problem there was. The remaining problems are easier. We may be ready for Morris's Law of Manifestation, where the time it takes to manifest whatever you can think of keeps halving. So whatever tech or medical breakthrough you're wishing for will arrive in 12 years now, not 25. Then if you don't get it, it arrives in just 6 more years. Then 3, then 2, then 1, then we reach the Singularity. So whatever all this is will certainly end by 2050. I just hope that whatever's on the other side has less suffering rather than more.

Sorry this got so long. I've been thinking about it for a long time.

title: Show HN: Klistra – A complete studio for spec-driven AI motion design and video
text:
As a solo-dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. Note that this was before AI-coded music videos went viral, back in the early days when the models were just getting good enough to make the result actually look good.

In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow into an easy to use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, web scraper and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. This way there is always a written specification that matches the render / build. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one time packs (Pro starting at $25/mo and packs at $12). Being a solo-dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

I created tutorials covering the basics. Mostly relying on the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic and for advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

You can see demo videos on the home page https://klistra.ai/ and on the tutorial pages. I would love to see what you make!

Some additional notes:

- After feedback from friends there is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Klistra can create images too.

Happy to hear what you think!

title: Re: Show HN: Cloudish – Cloud for agents to deploy con...
text:
Hi there HN, want to share a project in the works for five years. After working in Microsoft Research and then RStudio, I left to start Hal9 to build a WebML AI platform. Over five years I've learned a lot and pivoted many times, but we kept building the core infrastructure that runs docker containers. This infra became Cloudish and we just launched it.

Cloud providers today are designed to have a human in many steps, starting with sign-up and even talking to support or sales people to increase your quotas. In addition, most send you an invoice at the end of the month for whatever you consume. This design causes friction at best and a $10K surprise bill at most.

Cloudish starts with the agent, not the human. Agents running in Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Cursor, etc. can simply mint their own key by calling an API and deploy a docker container. Cloudish provides the build system, multiple instance types, logs for the build, an image registry, runtime logs, volume persistence and basic OIDC authentication. We achieve this by making the https://cloudish.ai/skill.md file the main interface to agents with an optional website https://www.cloudish.ai/ for humans to claim their projects, manage them and buy credits. Currently we top up with Stripe but have 402 payments in the not-so-distant roadmap.

Our main differentiator is ease of use for agents. We want to enable agents to deploy fully autonomously, so we created an open source benchmark to measure if agents can deploy to cloud providers without user intervention (https://github.com/cloudishai/ai-deploy-bench) and we will keep measuring progress towards this over time.

We've been dogfooding this with various projects that run in Cloudish, here are some of our favorite ones:

- https://www.cloudish.ai: The website itself runs on cloudish.ai

- https://demo.cloudish.app: This one shows how you can build and deploy a simplified Lovable clone that uses a docker sandbox to run Claude Code and then deploy the websites back to Cloudish

- https://awesomedataviz.com: A list of data viz projects

- https://puzzle.cloudish.app: Uses computer vision to solve puzzles

- https://whatislocalhost.com: Explains what is localhost

- https://lightpaths.cloudish.app: An R ray tracing demo created with rayrender

- https://neurosciencebook.com: Under development, chapter 1 written

title: Re: Show HN: Take Voyager 1 apart, down to a single me...
text:
I'd be fascinated to know the exact nature of the failure. What analog processes cause a CMOS memory IC that we like to think of as being discrete to be consistently wrong at reading its stored values? I'd like to know all the way down to the interaction between the gates and traces. Did some pathway erode due to constant interchange of charge carriers? Did thermal cycles or stress cause one of the mechanical interconnects on the package to fracture and no longer conduct? If so, which one?

According to AI, one type of failure mode in those early aerospace CMOS chips was sudden parasitic current in the PNPN junction being caused by a high energy particle, shorting paths to ground melting metal. Though that sounds rare. Another option is a total ionizing dose of radiation over time, which creates electron-hole pairs in the gate oxide, leading to trapped positive charge. That makes NMOS get closer and closer to turning on when they shouldn't, and PMOS requiring more voltage to turn on. It's fascinating to me that there came a specific moment in time when the chip managed to work, and the next clock cycle it didn't. I'd love to see the I_D vs. V_GS charts showing a before and after. So I had Claude make a plausible approximation. You can too by asking your AI agent of choice by basically just pasting in my comment!
